title: From geometry to dynamics: Learning overdamped Langevin dynamics from sparse observations with geometric constraints
topic: General Machine Learning->Sequential, Network, and Time Series Modeling
claim: Existing temporal and geometric inference methods each fail under sparse sampling; geometry-guided path augmentation combines their strengths to fix this.
layout: 6 panels in grid, A–E top, F bottom pipeline left-to-right, boxed titles
description: A multi-panel figure of rounded boxes with grey titles. Panel A shows temporal methods: a noisy limit-cycle trajectory with purple observation dots, two time series with increments dX marked, and a drift estimator written as a conditional expectation with teal and purple bars. Panel B shows geometric methods: an invariant density surface, a potential landscape and a gradient vector field, with a density-estimation row below. Panel C has a line plot of error rising with inter-observation interval, next to a ring-shaped point cloud with a path highlighted in yellow and magenta. Panel D shows grey sampled bridges between two observations. Panel E stacks three bridge examples: naive drift, Brownian and Ornstein-Uhlenbeck. Panel F, along the bottom, runs left to right through the metric, the geodesic and the constrained bridge. Magenta text marks the key steps.
caption: Temporal and geometric perspectives for discovering stochastic dynamics and proposed inference with geometrically guided augmentation. (A.) Temporal methods consider the time-ordering of observations {Ok}K τ |Xt = x⟩. (B.) Geometric methods assume a conservative drift f(x) = −∇V (x) as the gradient of a potential. (C.) With increasing inter-observation interval τ performance of temporal methods degrades because Euclidean distances ignore the curvature of the latent continuous path between consecutive observations. (D.) Path augmentation alternates between state estimation - by sampling diffusion bridges for each inter-observation interval - and drift inference. (E.) Commonly used path augmentation methods employ Brownian or Ornstein-Uhlenbeck bridges that increasingly deviate from the unobserved path as τ grows. (lower) Illustration of the ground truth (neon green) and geodesic (magenta) continuous path between two observations and of that assumed during inference with Gaussian likelihood (yellow line). (F.) Geometrically guided augmentation approximates first the metric induced by the invariant density, constructs geodesics connecting consecutive observations, and samples geometrically constrained diffusion bridges.
abstract: How can we learn the laws underlying the dynamics of stochastic systems when their trajectories are sampled sparsely in time? Existing methods either require temporally resolved high-frequency observations, or rely on geometric arguments that apply only to conservative systems, limiting the range of dynamics they can recover. Here, we present a new framework that reconciles these two perspectives by reformulating inference as a stochastic control problem. Our method uses geometry-driven path augmentation, guided by the geometry in the system's invariant density to reconstruct likely trajectories and infer the underlying dynamics without assuming specific parametric models. Applied to overdamped Langevin systems, our approach accurately recovers stochastic dynamics even from extremely undersampled data, outperforming existing methods in synthetic benchmarks. This work demonstrates the effectiveness of incorporating geometric inductive biases into stochastic system identification methods.
